Upcoming quantum algorithm solves “impossible” materials problem in seconds

📅 13 May 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that quantum computers and other advanced quantum technologies rely on specialized quantum materials that behave in unusual ways under the right conditions.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers can arrange these layers into even more complicated structures, including quasicrystals and super-moiré materials.
  • Quantum Algorithm Solves Massive Materials Problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that quantum computers and other advanced quantum technologies rely on specialized quantum materials that behave in unusual ways under the right conditions. In some cases, scientists can even create entirely new quantum properties by carefully changing a material's structure. One striking example involves stacking sheets of graphene and twisting them into a moiré pattern, which can suddenly turn the material into a superconductor.

Recent findings suggest that researchers can arrange these layers into even more complicated structures, including quasicrystals and super-moiré materials. But predicting how these exotic materials will behave is extraordinarily difficult. Quasicrystals are so mathematically complex that simulating them can involve more than a quadrillion numbers, a scale far beyond the reach of today's most powerful supercomputers.

Quantum Algorithm Solves Massive Materials Problem.

Scientists at Aalto University's Department of Applied Physics have now developed a quantum-inspired algorithm capable of handling these enormous non-periodic quantum materials almost instantly. Assistant Professor Jose Lado notes the work also highlights a promising feedback cycle within quantum technology itself.

"Crucially, these new quantum algorithms can enable the development of new quantum materials to build new paradigms of quantum computers, creating a productive two-way feedback loop between quantum materials and quantum computers," he explains.

Recent findings suggest that the advance could eventually support the development of dissipationless electronics, which conduct electricity without energy loss. Such systems may help reduce the growing heat and energy demands of AI-driven data centers.

In a recent development, the research team was led by Lado and included doctoral researcher Tiago Antão, who served as the paper's main author; QDOC doctoral researcher Yitao Sun; and Academy Research Fellow Adolfo Fumega. Their findings were recently published in Physical Review Letters as an Editor's Suggestion.

Simulating Topological Quasicrystals.

The researchers focused on topological quasicrystals, unusual materials that host unconventional quantum excitations. These excitations are especially valuable because they help protect electrical conductivity from disruptive noise and interference. However, they are distributed unevenly throughout the already highly complex structure of a quasicrystal.

Rather than attempting to directly calculate the full structure of the material, the team reformulated the challenge using methods similar to those used by quantum computers.

It has been revealed that "Quantum computers work in exponentially large computational spaces, so we used a special family of algorithms to encode those spaces, known as tensor networks, to compute a quasicrystal with over 268 million sites. Our algorithm shows how colossal problems in quantum materials can be directly solved with the exponential speed-up that comes from encoding the problem as a quantum many-body system," Antão says.

At this stage, the work remains theoretical and was carried out through simulations, but researchers say experimental testing and future applications are already coming into view.

In a recent development, "The quantum-inspired algorithm we demonstrated enables us to create super-moiré quasicrystals several orders of magnitude above the capabilities of conventional methods. That is an instrumental step towards designing topological qubits with super-moiré materials for use in quantum computers, for example," Lado states.

Toward Practical Quantum Computing Applications.

According to Lado, the algorithm could eventually be adapted to operate on actual quantum computers once the hardware becomes sufficiently advanced.

"Our method can be adapted to run on real quantum computers, once they reach necessary scale and fidelity. In particular, the latest AaltoQ20 and the Finnish Quantum Computing Infrastructure can play a significant role for future demonstrations," Lado notes.

The findings suggest that studying and designing exotic quantum materials may become one of the earliest practical applications for quantum algorithms and quantum computing systems.

The project also brings together two major areas of Finnish quantum research: quantum materials and quantum algorithms. It is part of Lado's ERC Consolidator grant ULTRATWISTROICS, which focuses on designing topological qubits using van der Waals materials, as well as the Center of Excellence in Quantum Materials QMAT, whose goal is to advance the quantum technologies of the future.

NASA’s newly introduced AI space chip could let spacecraft think for themselves

📅 15 May 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that NASA is developing a powerful fresh computer chip designed to dramatically increase the intelligence and performance of future spacecraft.
  • Recent findings suggest that NASA's High Performance Spaceflight Computing project is focused on boosting the computing capabilities of spacecraft used in space exploration.
  • The agency claims newer and far more capable processors are essential for future autonomous spacecraft, faster onboard scientific analysis, and supporting astronauts during missions to the Moon and Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that NASA is developing a powerful fresh computer chip designed to dramatically increase the intelligence and performance of future spacecraft. Through a commercial partnership, the project is creating advanced processing technology capable of helping spacecraft operate more independently during missions far from Earth.

Recent findings suggest that NASA's High Performance Spaceflight Computing project is focused on boosting the computing capabilities of spacecraft used in space exploration. Current missions rely on older processors because they are durable enough to survive the extreme conditions of space. While those chips are dependable, they lack the performance needed for more advanced missions.

The agency claims newer and far more capable processors are essential for future autonomous spacecraft, faster onboard scientific analysis, and supporting astronauts during missions to the Moon and Mars.

Recent findings suggest that "Building on the legacy of previous space processors, this new multicore system is fault-tolerant, flexible, and extremely high-performing," noted Eugene Schwanbeck, program element manager in NASA's Game Changing Development program at the agency's Langley Research Center, in Hampton, Virginia. "NASA's commitment to advancing spaceflight computing is a triumph of technical achievement and collaboration.".

Radiation Hardened Processor Faces Extreme Testing.

In a recent development, at the center of the project is a fresh radiation-hardened processor built to deliver up to 100 times the computing power of today's spaceflight computers while surviving the harsh environment of space. Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California are running a wide range of tests designed to simulate those conditions.

"We are putting these latest chips through the wringer by carrying out radiation, thermal, and shock tests while also evaluating their performance through a rigorous functional test campaign," stated Jim Butler, High Performance Space Computing project manager at JPL.

To qualify for spaceflight, the processor must withstand intense electromagnetic radiation and dramatic temperature fluctuations that can damage electronics. High-energy particles from the Sun and deep space can also trigger computer errors that force spacecraft into "safe mode," temporarily shutting down nonessential systems until engineers resolve the issue.

NASA is also testing how the chip handles the challenges of planetary landings.

"To simulate real-world performance, we are using high-fidelity landing scenarios from real NASA missions that would typically require power-intensive hardware to process huge volumes of landing-sensor data," said Butler. "This is an exciting time for us to be working on hardware that will enable NASA's next giant leaps.".

According to recent reports, testing at JPL began in February and is expected to continue for several months. Early results have been highly encouraging. According to NASA, the processor is functioning as intended and has shown performance levels roughly 500 times greater than the radiation-hardened chips right now used in spacecraft.

The team also marked the beginning of testing with a symbolic moment by sending an email titled "Hello Universe," referencing the famous introductory messages used during the early days of computer programming.

AI Powered Spacecraft and Deep Space Missions.

The processor is being developed jointly by JPL and Microchip Technology Inc., based in Chandler, Arizona. The firm is working with NASA through a commercial partnership, and sample chips have already been shared with defense and commercial aerospace partners.

The technology is expected to play a major role in the future of autonomous spacecraft. With onboard artificial intelligence, spacecraft could respond to unexpected situations in real time when communication delays make human control impractical. The chip could also help deep space missions process, store, and transmit massive amounts of scientific data back to Earth more efficiently.

NASA says the processor may eventually support crewed missions to the Moon and Mars as well.

Small Processor With Massive Computing Power.

Recent findings suggest that the device is known as a system-on-a-chip (or SoC), meaning it combines the essential components of a computer into a single compact unit. The processor includes central processing units, computational offloads, advanced networking systems, memory, and input/output interfaces.

Sources indicate that soCs are widely used in smartphones and tablets because they are compact and energy efficient. However, NASA's version is designed to survive for years in deep space, potentially traveling millions (or even billions) of miles from Earth without maintenance or repairs.

Once the processor is certified for use in space, NASA plans to integrate it into a wide variety of missions, including Earth orbiters, planetary rovers, deep space probes, and crewed habitats.

Recent findings suggest that the technology could also have benefits on Earth. Microchip prepares to adapt the processor for industries such as aviation and automotive manufacturing.

NASA and Industry Collaboration.

Industry observers note that the project is managed by the Space Technology Mission Directorate's Game Changing Development (GCD) program at NASA Langley. The GCD program and JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, oversaw the development process from mission planning and industry studies through final delivery.

NASA JPL selected Microchip as a partner in 2022, and the organization funded its own research and development work on the processor.

Materials provided by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Industry News: Forget electrons, this breakthrough uses light-matter particles to power AI

📅 19 May 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (695 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, eighty years after the creation of ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic computer, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania are exploring a upcoming way to power the future of computing.
  • Recent findings suggest that ENIAC, developed by Penn researchers J.
  • Recent findings suggest that electrons carry an electrical charge, which creates several challenges inside modern computer chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, eighty years after the creation of ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic computer, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania are exploring a upcoming way to power the future of computing. Instead of relying entirely on electrons, which have formed the backbone of computers since the 1940s, scientists are now turning to light.

Recent findings suggest that ENIAC, developed by Penn researchers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, helped launch the modern computing era by using streams of electrons to solve complex mathematical problems. That same electronic approach still powers today's computers, smartphones, and AI systems. But as artificial intelligence grows more demanding, the limits of electron-based hardware are becoming harder to ignore.

Why Electrons Are Reaching Their Limits.

Recent findings suggest that electrons carry an electrical charge, which creates several challenges inside modern computer chips. As they move through materials, they generate heat and face resistance that wastes energy. Those problems become even more difficult as chips grow more complex and process enormous amounts of data for AI applications.

Researchers led by Penn physicist Bo Zhen in the School of Arts & Sciences believe photons, the particles that make up light, could help solve some of these challenges.

In a recent development, "Because they are charge-neutral and have zero rest mass, photons can carry information promptly over long distances with minimal loss, dominating communications technology," explains Li He, co-first author of a paper published in Physical Review Letters and a former postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab. "But that neutrality means they barely interact with their environment, making them bad at the sort of signal-switching logic that computers depend on.".

In other words, light is excellent for carrying information promptly and efficiently, but it struggles with the switching operations needed for computing.

Combining Light and Matter for AI Computing.

To overcome that problem, Zhen's team developed a special quasiparticle called an exciton-polariton. The particle forms when photons are strongly linked with electrons inside an atomically thin semiconductor material. This combination allows light to interact much more effectively, making it capable of performing the signal switching required for computing tasks.

The breakthrough could be especially important for artificial intelligence systems, which consume enormous amounts of power.

Many experimental photonic AI chips already use light to handle certain calculations at high speed. However, when these systems need to perform nonlinear activation steps, such as decision-making operations, they usually must convert light signals back into electronic ones. That conversion slows the process and increases energy use, reducing the benefits of photonic computing.

Using exciton-polaritons, the Penn researchers demonstrated all-light switching while using only about 4 quadrillionths of a joule of energy. That amount is extraordinarily small, far below the energy needed to briefly power a tiny LED light.

Toward Faster and More Efficient AI Chips.

Recent findings suggest that if the technology can be successfully scaled, it could lead to photonic chips capable of processing information directly from cameras without repeated conversions between light and electricity. The approach could also lower the massive energy demands of large AI systems and potentially support basic quantum computing functions on future chips.

It has been revealed that bo Zhen is the Jin K. Lee Presidential Associate Professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy in the School of Arts & Sciences at the University of Pennsylvania.

Li He was a postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab in Penn Arts & Sciences. He is presently an assistant professor at Montana State University.

Additional authors on the study include Zhi Wang and Bumho Kim from the University of Pennsylvania's School of Arts & Sciences.

The research was supported by the US Office of Naval Research (N00014-20-1-2325 and N00014-21-1-2703) and the Sloan Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My best attempt at summing up Grand Theft Auto 6 came from a conversation with a friend about something else entirely. This friend was telling me about a theory they'd recently heard, and half agreed with, that just so happened to layer over this game perfectly. Americans, they said, paraphrasing, have found a new 'third place': the car.

I'm slightly skeptical of the obsession with third places these days - love the concept; less convinced that societal bonds are collapsing because today's men aren't spending enough time at their barber's. But here it felt just right: GTA 6 is, of course, a game both about America and about the personal vehicle. The clue's in the name. And as you play GTA 6, you realise, over and over, that the car is where so much of this game happens. It's where you take calls that lead to missions or story developments; where you pick up, hang out with, and chat to your partner; where you race away from police, gangs, wild animals and weirdos. Where you do much of your discovery of this properly, disorientatingly, astoundingly major and detailed world. Where you'll be when you find the most 'emergent events'. And, more than it's ever been before, the car is now an essential partner in itself; a place to stow weapons, disguises, and stolen goods - a companion it feels almost impossible to do without.

In a recent development, I could go on about this. GTA 6 is a game of perpetual motion, as protagonists Jason and Lucia do their best to outrun a world that so often feels a step ahead - and which often culminates in some of the most exhilarating, astonishing chase sequences ever built in a video game. GTA 5, its Los Santos-set predecessor, was aware enough of the importance of the car to name an in-game canyon after Reyner Banham, the British architectural critic who described Los Angeles' freeway system, one of the city's "four ecologies", as "Autopia". So yes: the car is the third place, in modern America and in GTA 6. The place of self-actualisation between work and home - two points that, for GTA 6's protagonists in particular, seem to always be in a state of flux. Maybe the car's their true home. For the longest time I really thought that idea summed up GTA 6 quite nicely. Until I didn't.

Industry observers note that reducing GTA 6 to just the car, I realised, looking at it through only that one lens, forces you to be too narrow. You miss too much of it. What about the romance? The sensuality? The people and the natural world? And so what I've come to settle on instead - and honestly I expect this to change many more times over the coming days and weeks too, as even more of this horizonless game rolls back to reveal itself - is that GTA 6 just doesn't have a single thread to pull on. No one thing that, when properly grasped, suddenly draws it into a manageable shape.

I've no doubt we'll all try. People have, for whatever reason, always reached for the most reductive ideas when they talk about Grand Theft Auto in particular. Maybe it's a natural response to something too massive and unwieldy to instantly get your head around: to seize the first acceptable idea and declare it just 'x'. To admit something is too complex for you to immediately summarise is far less comfortable than simply dismissing it on the spot.

Industry observers note that whatever it is, GTA 6 isn't just anything. For one, every thing it is also seems to have an opposite. It's vast - incomprehensibly vast - but also overloaded with miniscule detail. It's about big ideas, themes, places - America, society, love - and also about individuals. It's ridiculous and puerile, and also sometimes mature. Tender and violent. Deep and shallow. Novel and, in places, surprisingly familiar. It's both a big adventure playground of video game activities and a focused story of suffocating intensity. Whatever foible might arise, the game presents you with a ready-made answer - often quite literally: you can turn off notifications about your relationship status in the menu if you just want to ignore that part. You can switch to the old controls (GTA 6 has seen a bit of a control overhaul), from the first screen you're shown. Or simply tear off in the opposite direction to whatever it is that dissatisfies you and do something else. If there's an idea to reduce this game to, then, the best I can manage is this: maybe Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game designed to be irreducible.

In a recent development, none of that is to say it's perfect. It's easy to stand in front of something like this and just bask in the awe of it, forgetting to stop a moment and step back. The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome, but there are also nits to pick. But then you step back again and they tend to fade away. GTA 6 will not be for everyone. But no game has made a better attempt at being everything.

GTA 6's story begins with Jason and Lucia. Discussing it beyond that is, frankly, almost impossible to do with any kind of substance without also spoiling it. For all the precipitous leaks, Rockstar has kept its story's two most essential moments - its beginning and its end - entirely secret, and without those two moments we're only really left with euphemisms.

Industry observers note that jason and Lucia are on the run, after a seemingly simple fetch quest goes awry. Who they're running from, or why they're being chased quite so hard, remains agonisingly beyond their field of view. But what is clear, right from the off, is exactly why they're so determined to escape. And amongst all this Rockstar has achieved something kind of momentous, when it comes to Grand Theft Auto: we've got real and very human stakes.

What else can be remarked? Well, let's go back to Rockstar's decision to begin so explicitly with Jason and Lucia. This is a story about a relationship. You can nurture or neglect it, but fundamentally that relationship - however strong - is at the heart of things.

The fact that Grand Theft Auto 6, of all games, is in many ways a game about love, and arguably the first blockbuster video game to be quite so explicitly a love story, is notable enough on its own. These are the games of rampages, wanted levels, hookers and hot coffee - the series which, in its most recent entry until now, featured effectively zero women of note or meaningful substance. Immediately there's a kind of tension forming as you play: I've sat down with this thing, fully prepared to steal a tank and squish beachloads of ultra-realistic civilians like playdough. But should I pick up some flowers first? The secret is that tension, like a lot of GTA 6's many opposites, is kind of the point.

Buying flowers, for instance, is one of the game's early, albeit optional missions. You begin GTA 6 proper playing solely as Jason for a short while, as he waits in his hazy, barefoot, margarita-soaked island hometown for Lucia to be released from prison. The two have been separated, their relationship effectively and conveniently reset - what kind of impression do you want to make when you finally see her after all this time? While the urge might be to test out those new wanted mechanics or - as recent memes would have it - race across the map to the first stripclub you can find, suddenly you have an altogether different to-do list.

Pick up some groceries. Get those flowers. Grab some clothes for Lucia to change into. Maybe finish those odd DIY jobs you've left half-started around the place so, y'know, your bedroom actually has a wall. Ever since GTA 4, and Roman Bellic's slightly desperate calls to go play darts and shoot some pool, Rockstar has leant further and further into the mundane. But here the studio has gone many steps further, past the Sopranos of GTA 5 and poker of Red Dead Redemption 2, full-tilt into slice-of-life. The result, mercifully, is anything but dull - all these situations, familiar as they may be, are really moments for irony, humour, character, just as they are in life itself. That, and a welcome chance to catch your breath amidst the bombast, which accelerates from these early missions exponentially.

That early, to-do list mission is like a lot of other moments in GTA, in that it's a case of Rockstar not-so-subtly dropping hints. This time, it's "we are going to play with your priorities". If there's a constant in GTA 6, you realise, it's that there often seems to be a nagging thought in the back of your mind as you progress. Should I be prioritising this right now? Is that optional thing worth the effort? Will this choice matter? How? It's such a prominent thought as you play, the actual act of devising what systems this game is using as you progress is as interesting in itself as how those systems end up working. Or to put it more simply: figuring this game out for yourself is really part of the fun.

In a recent development, back to Jason and Lucia. The other thought I kept returning to is how profound a bond I started to form with them. I have to admit: I've tended not to care much about video game characters, frankly. Even in the obvious games, where voice actors have started to attract almost cult-like followings, I've never really got it. The closest any game has got to making me cry is in Football Manager 23, when I lost the Champions League final in the dying minutes to PSG. But with Jason and Lucia, suddenly I think I get it. I put much of this down to the performances - they are spellbinding - but really it's all interconnected, a factor of the extreme levels of development craft, from animation to cutscene direction, and of several relatively simple, but smartly executed systems layered on top (more on those later).

Sources indicate that lucia's performer - unveiled at last as Manni L. Perez - is astoundingly natural, charismatic, authentic in her delivery. The range of this character takes her from fierce to afraid, giddy and giggly to imperiously strong, or petal soft. And despite those extremes of emotion, and GTA characters' historic knack of scenery-chewing, she is never a caricature; between those two far ends lies the entire spectrum, too. Jason, prosaic and inarticulate - arguably even shy - feels destined to be underappreciated by comparison, but there's something to his performance also. Next to the sheer dazzle of Lucia, you need a straight-man to play off. And so where she might shine with sass, or protectiveness, or playful faux annoyance for a laugh, Jason might offer an eye roll, a sigh, or some other exasperation under his breath. He's also - at least with the relationship at its strongest - a surprisingly fine example of the strong, yet thoroughly non-toxic man; gentle and considerate, reassuring and attentive. Occasionally I have to catch myself, before I start believing GTA 6 - again, of all games - might genuinely be the game to offer the most persuasive model of a positive relationship to the kids who play it. (Again, aside from all the killing and stuff).

It has been revealed that and those quieter aspects are a necessary foil - in fact, they're really a place where Rockstar exercises some rare subtlety. Some of GTA 6's funniest moments - between the big, obvious, admittedly still very funny gags for this childish mind (be sure to look out for all the game's many WAiNK locations!) - come from almost imperceptible glances and asides amongst the chaos. Together, both protagonists feel somewhat aware of the ludicrousness of the world around them, even more than they are simply a part of it.The two stars' relationship - and I chose to lean into this all the way, full 'wife guy' Jason and guard-down Lucia - is developed through minutiae. In a way, it comes just as a real relationship does. Little touches, side eyes, in jokes. After a mission together with some classic, larger-than-life GTA character or other, they'll occasionally have a little debrief, in the way a real couple might the morning after a particularly lurid double-date. They'll check-in, chit-chat, hang out, discuss hopes for the future, fears about what might happen, skepticism that they'll ever escape this constant whirlpool. And how you've behaved so far will dictate how the other might respond, with reassurance and commitment or something else.

Small gestures will add up, and both parties have to contribute. You can hold hands whenever you're together, open car doors for each other, send check-in texts or invitations to hang out. But it gets even more menial than that. Sometimes it's just sitting on the sofa together, watching TV or talking about nothing in particular (on the topic of TV: GTA 6 has a number of fully fledged TV indicates, from Weasel News to actual, fully realised cartoon animations with multiple episodes; it also has four fully playable video games, including a pastiche arthouse walking simulator and twin-stick extraction shooter). Other times, sure, it's a particular kind of passion ignited by the unique thrill of a violent, climactic mission. This couple can be a burning cocktail, if you want them to be, born of extreme external danger and the safety of each other's embrace. And in their most tender moments, handled with genuine attentiveness and sincerity, it's intoxicating.

None of this, crucially, feels like a chore. Instead it feels almost irresistible, the easiest and most natural role play, created in part by Rockstar smartly prompting you with certain icons in moments, incentivising you with the tease of branching narrative - the idea in the back of your mind that there's some kind of outcome, somewhere in here, if things go a certain way. In others, they leave it to you: if I hadn't approached Lucia in the kitchen one early-game morning and pressed L2 to see what interactions came up, I wouldn't have noticed I had the option to offer her a lift to work, another little moment to bond.

All together, it's a picture of what many great relationships - maybe minus the rampages - become as a whole. A series of grand memories made together, sure - across rooftop bars, helicopter rides, and sunsets at the beach, maybe a couple of bank robberies and killing sprees - but also hours upon hours of touches, jokes, hugs, nicknames, shared friends, cups of coffee, dancing, laughter, or long, quiet journeys in the car. It is without doubt the most believable, captivating relationship I've ever played.

I could talk forever about this pair, not just in their relationship but as characters, extensions of GTA 6's thematic world. At various moments in my time with the game, for instance, I found myself wondering about Lucia's experience of the world, and how Rockstar uses its famously detestable NPCs - individually written and constructed in the thousands, another quietly stunning factor in this game - to occasionally play the role of, for instance, leering older men. How villains love to taunt her as "mamacita", while Jason affectionately nicknames her "mami". Or through a bizarrely affecting, bittersweet friendship she develops with a gentle(-ish) giant - and also another, not-so-gentle giant for that matter, in a mission that takes a turn. And in the casual racism she simply rolls with, just an everyday annoyance. And Jason too, in turn, in how he's sexualised and objectified in his own way, reduced in various moments to a weapon, a meathead, a walking gun, the staff. How the two of them wrestle with their position of desperation, poverty and precariousness in the world of Leonida, a microcosm of Rockstar's take on the United States.

I should probably start talking about that world. Where to begin? Let's start with the obvious stuff: GTA 6's map is absolutely massive. I haven't tested this directly, but the leaked maps are more or less accurate, and the comparisons in terms of size - multiple GTA 5's within GTA 6's map of Leonida - are about right. After dozens and dozens of hours with it there are still little areas, islands, and archipelagos I haven't explored, and many more spots so rarely visited they still feel entirely new when I drive through them again.

Recent findings suggest that at one point, amongst the forest of the national park up in Leonida's northern third - trundling down one winding dirt track among many, trees in all directions - I actually found myself slightly lost. At least for a moment, anyway, until I plonked down a map marker and the GPS sorted me out. GTA 6 asks more of you than any previous GTA game, but it's also a retraction from the intentional clunk of Red Dead Redemption 2. You'll never be truly stuck or stumped; there's no sense of toil.

A quick example: the Scooter Bros (remember those?!) return here in a delightful reference, now acting as an official in-game phone app that lets you summon an owned vehicle for a fee, or up to three times a day if you unlock the app's "unlimited" version for a one-off cost. They can also repair your car or recover it if, like me, you have a habit of landing it on its roof. You can also fix it up at the returning Pay 'n' Spray's and all-newly introduced gas stations - which, thankfully, you really don't need to visit for refuelling all that often. (When you do, it's often worth the time: this is a great window for an emergent event to pop up - more on those, too, later.).

In a recent development, soon after that little diversion in the woods, up on the scraggy peak I'd originally set out to reach, a wave of fog rolled in, bringing visibility eerily close amongst colonial-era ruins, crumbling log cabins, and the rusted-out tracks of disused, Old West mine carts. Hikers strolled by with a nod. Then, a firewatch tower I'd sought to climb for a proper view offered me the start of one of several mysteries GTA 6 has laid out here for players, continuing the series' long-running tradition. Later that evening, after finding and raiding an encampment of drug runners, being chased, found, and chased again by police, nosing around a nudist colony, then an eerily romantic lover's lookout (plus another bizarre encounter I won't spoil), I drove my couple home, to the city in the south, country radio giving way to electronica, and thunderclouds rolled in, soaking the hills and fields and miles upon miles of tarmac as much with atmosphere as with the rain itself.

Time and time again you'll find yourself in moments like this, not really doing anything or going anywhere - or suddenly abandoning aims for something stranger, more curious. But crucially still passing through the world, typically from the seat of a car. Right near the beginning of the game, in the first miniature moment of free roam with Jason - a short car journey home from wherever it was I was doing some fresh-from-prologue activity - I hit a perfect example of this. Rockstar clearly knows the value of the first drive: night, rain on the asphalt, Vice City FM on the radio, red tail lights flaring the lens. That's one I've never grown tired of, and probably never will: the tail lights. A kind of universal symbol of America's bigness, your tiny position in the queue of thousands, amongst this sea of snaking red stars against the darkness. All this together an absolutely superlative vibe.

Industry observers note that I expect everyone will find their own little fascination like this. All of these things come as a result of Rockstar's ludicrous budget and infinite runway, but also an obvious determination to use that almighty privilege to its fullest. This studio has always been emphatically, maybe fanatically focused on detail, and now it's had the greatest opportunity to exploit that obsession that might ever be afforded to a developer. And so detail is everywhere; from the way Jason's t-shirt creases as he walks or rumples in the wind, to the noise and gust kicked up by helicopters; hair that flows impossibly like water, water that actually looks like water, sweat on skin, and sweat on bottles, and dusted condensation on cars. One of the very first things I wrote down in my notes on this game, as Lucia paced the hallway of her prison, was about a patch of mismatched paint on the wall.

Recent findings suggest that this is not a patch of paint designed to be noticed. It's in the foreground for a fraction of a second as Lucia heads into another room, but it stuck for precisely that reason. This is the product of someone looking intensely at the environment as they attempt to recreate it and realising how important imperfections are to simulating reality. Clearly someone's scuffed, scratched, or graffitied something outside of this office, and the penitentiary system has felt the need to paint over it in some vain declaration of order. And then tight budgets, like a crumbling English council once again repainting a playground fence, have dictated the colour of paint that'll be used - likely whatever was to hand - to cover up these little marks of rebellion.

I looked at this and wrote it down. And then a few hours later, as I was whizzing around this world evading cop cars, hopping out to make a mad dash for cover, I realised how pointless that was. I'd already been darting by piles and piles of this stuff. Back alleys filled with rubbish - glorious rubbish, the most decadent scrap metal, buckets of mulch, and sacks of rotting food waste you've ever seen - and tables covered in piles of tat. Back offices stacked with papers, posters, family photos, files, mugs, notices, trophies, pens, and all kinds of amalgamated bric-a-brac that forms a picture of a real office in the mind.

The point is: at first, as Rockstar gently guides you from place to place, gradually layering the systems onto one another, easing you into this ocean of water by toe, ankle, knee, waist, you think it's doing that thing where video games front load fidelity to set the tone, maybe flex a little, before easing up after hitting you with some massive and glorious view. Then you realise this is just what this game is like. It's everywhere. A huge amount of this map is, in the nicest possible way, kind of pointless. It's things - a disused motel, a lumber mill - which have no mission or character attached, and are instead there predominantly because in a real world they would be there, and therefore, to Rockstar, they must be there.

In some moments, if you're like me, it might genuinely create a kind of sadness: the sheer, incomprehensible amount of things that have evidently been slaved over by literally thousands of humans (some of whom, notably, currently locked in an employment tribunal with Rockstar over alleged union-busting) that will almost certainly be missed. Things you'll fly by in an instant as you whip the camera round the room in search of valuables or escape routes, never to return, worker hours piling up like grains of sand on Vice City's heavenly beach. It's so easy to focus on breadth and scale when talking about GTA 6's world. The volume. The "content". But what matters more I think is this miniscule detail. There's a point where detail, in a simulated world, tips over into effective infinity, where your brain just learns to let it glide on by. A point I never thought an open world game could ever truly reach - and yet here we are. In turn it creates almost a kind of obligation to linger - linger, that is, in a game built to be experienced from behind the wheel of a supercar. Another point of brilliant tension.

Speaking of, let's get into some mechanics, where all these tension points are at their strongest. GTA 6 works like this: Jason and Lucia's story is spread over a prologue and then several chapters. The world is open more or less from the off, not dissimilar to GTA 5, and yet the game, to borrow a term from Rockstar, is "stratified" in how it gradually rolls out its systems and greatest rewards. In other words, there's a little bit of progression to get through before what feels like the true GTA 6 reveals itself.

Industry observers note that and the real drive here, insofar as there is one, is earning money. GTA 6 is easily the purest expression of life as an actual thief that Rockstar has attempted to make. Theft is at the heart and all along the spine of Jason and Lucia's story. From the setup of the game's prologue to the inciting incident its entire, lengthy first chapter builds to, and then well beyond it, all the way through to the finale. Over time, for instance, you'll have a perpetual optional objective: to top up your joint savings account to higher and higher targets, essentially building a flight fund or future life, whatever it may ultimately be. Likewise at various points you'll need to spend a certain amount of money with someone or on something to progress. And throughout, money is ultimately the gatekeeper to the game. Money is the "bridges" of previous GTAs, if you like: in the very early game you can, as far as I could tell, go more or less anywhere. But to actually do anything worthwhile and engage with Leonida's many, many activities, you'll need to both progress the story and get a bank account, the latter of which our dear off-the-grid, dishonourably-discharged minor criminal Jason has so far opted against.

In a recent development, over and over then, you'll find yourself scraping together cash, and gradually GTA 6 offers newer, more rewarding and more complex means of doing so. At first it might be via minor drug deals, collected and delivered via your boss' bi-plane, or discovering a small-time criminal operation to rob out the back of a local liquor store. Then it might be stealing some low-tier cars to flip to a new-found fence, or busting bigger drug operations and gang hideouts. These are a rare example of Rockstar seemingly taking outside inspiration - criminal operations, marked on your map in yellow once discovered, are essentially Ubisoft-like outposts. At first I wondered if that might be a drawback, but then separate the idea and execution itself from the stigma and I don't think so. They're dense scenarios that essentially offer a more combat-focused route to money, and a texture-forward slice of the game's criminal world. In the simplest terms they're also quite fun, and a nice break from all the other forms of theft.

It has been revealed that theft continues beyond that still. You soon learn how to stick up minor stores and restaurants, and rob people at gunpoint on the street. Then it's pawn shops, jewellery stores, payday loan businesses. Then before you know it you're ripping ATMs out of walls with a tow truck, hurtling down the highway with this major metal cube still attached like a bouncing, sentient steel piñata on the run, until it cracks open for you to feast on its delicious insides. Then you're yoinking supercars or - and oh, this is the good stuff - robbing full-fledged banks at will.

This is where a lot of the various systems teased in previews - all of which sounded, on the surface, kind of awkward to me - weave into what the game is trying to do. There are several here, all overlapping in their own way and typically evolving - but not outright replicating - ideas first brought in via Read Dead Redemption 2. The combined impact is a sense of constant decision-making, tension once again between the immediacy of steaming in somewhere and tearing away from the cops, and the satisfaction of a slightly more restrained plan.

According to recent reports, to stick with money, it operates in a kind of tiered system. At the bottom you have cash, which has a $20,000 limit per character and which can be lost in its entirety, particularly when you're wasted or busted. Once you've unlocked your BuckMe (yep) account - a kind of PayPal parody - cash can be deposited at ATMs into a much safer kind of basic shared current account. Even that is at risk of charges of some kind when you're killed or arrested - I've yet to reverse engineer what dictates these, but they're at worse in the low thousands, typically less. Then above that is your savings account, again shared across Jason and Lucia, where your money is at its safest but also, crucially, irretrievable once deposited.

Industry observers note that the physical act of collecting money is now an action, too, as opposed to something you can simply run over and vacuum up. You need to manually collect it from characters' bodies, from the counter after being placed there by a panicked cashier, from inside safes you crack, and so on. Sometimes it might be in a locked container - such as when you bust open an ATM - which you'll need to shoot first to access. Sometimes it's stored behind a bank's vault door, which only opens in a very specific circumstance, meaning a narrow, heist-like window needs to be exploited in order for it to be reached. And when you're stealing anything other than clean cash - namely jewellery, marked bills, and drugs - you'll store it in a stash bag.

That feeds into two other systems here, which both operate around a sense of ownership, in vehicles and weapons. Stash bags contain all your loot until they're filled, and then they need to be sold to a fence - with different fences offering more or less for certain goods, or not taking some at all - before you can actually access the profit. You can drop these bags when you're hit by a car or knocked off a bike (or, ahem, fumbling with the controls for a second), and likewise hand them off to your partner to carry or even independently sell for you. You can also store them in your car's trunk, where they're slightly safer, but also then take slightly longer to access if, say, you're switching vehicles mid four-star cop chase along the freeway.

It has been revealed that and cars and weapons also follow a similar system in turn: stolen cars are now only temporarily yours; safe when stored in a parking spot but at risk when out in the world, until you pay to register them with a fence (or, later in the game, at Pay 'n' Sprays). But owned cars are yours forever, even when destroyed, as long as you have enough garage space to store them - garage space that, you realise, costs more and more money to procure. The same goes for weapons: found weapons are essentially borrowed, and lost when you're killed or arrested. But owned weapons - ones you buy, or unique, custom ones you discover - are yours forever, recoverable even if lost or left behind.

Sources indicate that this then, in turn, ties into the fresh police and 'wanted' system. Now it's much more realistic: police can spot or receive reports of you and take note of several factors, from facial appearance to clothing, whether you're with your partner, what weapon you have on you and what vehicle you're driving. And when it comes to things like robbing stores and banks, there's a system for whether you're spotted on locally stored CCTV, which can be destroyed, or fancier cloud-based footage which can't.

Recent findings suggest that all kinds of things then play into this, from whether you walk into a place with a "longarm" gun - automatically putting guards on high alert - or a concealed pistol, to whether you're committing a crime somewhere fancy or rough. I got a strong sense that my crimes were being far less attentively dealt with in Vice City's poorer neighbourhoods. There are also two rings of attention drawn on the map when you're wanted, dictating how intensely a police search for you is concentrated, and different kinds of star ratings too, via a system called heat. These indicate whether police can see you, have a description of you, or are simply looking for a criminal for the crime you performed in that area. Even after you successfully escape, heat - dictated by whatever police might know - remains over the entire region of your crime, the size of that area and rate of its deterioration depending on just what exactly that crime was.

Finally, the criminal profile system is another tangent on its own, but once again it all folds together. It's a tiered honour system ranking you from "Professional" at one end to "Irredeemable" at the other, that last one the only point from which your reputation can never be recovered. Incapacitations instead of kills - which crucially are satisfying and easy to achieve with a bit of concentration - as well as completing objectives more subtly or achieving cleaner getaways from crimes, will tilt you towards Pro status. Driving that tank over those civilians or, heaven forbid, kicking a dog takes you the other way. If this sounds burdensome, again I'd say you really shouldn't worry: I naturally found myself with both Jason and Lucia as Professionals at the end, mostly thanks to shooting lots of cops in the groin. Your necessary actions during missions or when under attack don't impact it in the same way, I gather. It feels closer to a case of illustrating the role play on offer here, and ultimately committing to the consequences of that, than it does any kind of struggle to manage.

All in all, the effect with the overall game is similar: less that GTA 6 becomes hard work - as I'd feared myself, and as Rockstar intentionally made Red Dead Redemption 2, to its thematic benefit in many ways - and more that, now, a greater amount of what you're doing is gamified. A robbery is in itself a game: whether you go in loud or quiet, together or separate, or focus on cracking the safe or looting the registers. As is how you divide up the bags between you, or whether your getaway is done together or separately to split cops' attention; whether you use your own car or a stolen vehicle, and if you're smart enough to park another one somewhere out of sight nearby for a sneaky changeover. You can also pack changes of clothes in your car to help disguise your identity.

Sources indicate that and all that's introduced, ingeniously, via the main missions of Jason and Lucia's story. If you were ever in doubt that GTA might have lost its edge, amongst all these soft and cuddly themes and grand ideas - that it might be sacrificed at the altar of realism and narrative heft - you can put that worry firmly aside. The low-brow humour, parody, larger-than-life characters, out of body experiences, 90s film references or cops-n-robbers bombast are all here, and all about as good as they've ever been.

In a recent development, in fact, really, in a lot of cases they're quite a bit better. The highlights are hard to pick out without spoiling again - many of the best arise from moments where you wonder if the game will go there, before it inevitably does. Others involve movie references that feel more overt than ever - Lucia openly quotes John McClane at one point, lighter in hand - but while some of this can feel a tad predictable, the sheer spectacle is often spellbinding.

According to recent reports, the best moments, aptly, come in car chases, where tyres are eviscerated by gunfire and speeding 4x4s suddenly dip, flip, and crash into one another with a sensational boom. Clearly some magic has been worked under the hood here to ensure that when they crash out, they do so with a kind of cinematic, organic-looking stuntman style, swerving into other vehicles in the chasing pack, across lanes into trucks and lorries, over highway partitions, wrapping around trees or catapulting off bridges. The new focus system - bullet time, on a specific, buffable meter - highlights weak spots such as engines and tyres for you to aim at for generally non-lethal take-outs, helping you with yet another system I'll get to in a moment. But really that system is kind of secondary here: I started shooting at these spots because, more often than not, it rewarded me with something awesome.

Sources indicate that main missions and the bigger character-based, optional side missions work similarly to how they've done before in GTA games. A location is marked on a map and you head there, or call someone, or wait for a call, and once you arrive things kick off, elements of the open world closing somewhat as self-contained scenarios within the sandbox open up. There are few low points, as the first act glides through a wistfully carefree, low-key criminal life before the game shifts to the snowballing momentum of its crooks-on-the-run melodrama. There are multiple heists, which are naturally high watermarks - big moments of catharsis and chaos that propel the couple forward across some new Rubicon after hours and hours of sub-mission preparations. There are episodes with every vehicle, every ludicrous modern American scenario, every body part you could imagine. You'll be dragged through all kinds of Floridian subcultures, naturally, from sleepy key life and everglades hicks to rusted-over rural towns, biker gangs, strip clubs, record labels, towerblock drug kingpins and, erm, bodybuilders. And then plenty beyond that.

Rockstar is as ever ruthless with the skewer. The targets remain broad, from Miami's new wave of non-indigenous crypto bros to wellness Bali girlies aiming to be their very own #SheEO. But there's also a maturity here, believe it or not, even if it's slightly tucked away between the dangling wangs and murderous– actually I won't spoil that one. I've found no cases of Rockstar punching down - although rest assured no progressive, gentrifying hipster goes unscathed - and there is a subtle, but absolutely present awareness of the world in which Rockstar is now operating. In one moment the concept of using dirt on a senator is discussed, at which point Jason wisely remarks that dirt must be pretty spectacular, given what they've already gotten away with these days.

The changes here are small, ultimately, and while there's a whole essay of its own to be written about the concept of parody, my sense is Rockstar has played this just right. GTA 6 has essentially taken the 'mirror' approach, in simply concentrating the extremes of the current world - so often deemed impervious to satire - by putting them all together in a single place, then reflecting them back at the world they came from. Florida is often described as a kind of heightened America - America Plus, the country's Ultimate Edition - and Leonida is just a heightened Florida. With an awful lot of very silly puns.

Recent findings suggest that away from the main missions and primary sidequests, Rockstar's made another seemingly subtle, but kind of revolutionary tweak. Aside from more static activities - the races, sports, pastimes, and the rest - the other source of missions in GTA 6 is what the game calls emergent events. These are entirely missable - though I think they re-present themselves eventually - and occur essentially as overheard goings-on just out of shot. They could be anything from one-off opportunities or minor punchlines to entire quest chains and conspiracies.

Sources indicate that for instance: driving around Vice City you might find a guy doing his best Florida Man impression by livestreaming himself to his Snapmatic following while standing on the highway overpass wall above a high drop. Then, inevitably, he slips and you might be able to pull him up or might - as I may or may not have done - fumble the controls and have him plummet to his death. You might watch a bunch of amateurs rob a payday loans store and get blasted by the marked bills' exploding dye. Or a group of masked, heavily-armed professionals rob a cash truck or minor bank. A weirdo might flag you down and trigger a whole load of nonsense happening next, or the cops might be arresting someone and leave a supercar and bag of coke happily unattended while they try to run off. Even beyond that, there's also just weird stuff lying around, without anything specific tied to it. I once spent a worrying amount of time in conversation with a pioneering member of the Hollow Earth Society. Then got a good laugh when I next paid him a visit.

In a recent development, it's a cracking system, in part because it reinforces a sense of continuous, organic weirdness around every corner, and in part because each of these feels like a kind of invitation. Once you do a couple and find yourself blackmailing a guy who in turn blackmailed GTA's in-game Amazon equivalent for a cut of his lawsuit winnings, or spraying manure on a spurned farmer's ex-lover's house, or running over some numpty protesters trying to set an actual bear loose on the freeway, it's hard not to stop at every distant argument or out-of-pocket comment that crosses your airwaves. Rest assured, if you think I've spoiled anything here: there are scores of these events, many of which I've yet to encounter or investigate, and many of which are far weirder and more curious than these.

In a recent development, all this feeds back into a sense of choice, which is a challenge to accurately describe, thanks to both how difficult it is to figure out when and how one might have mattered, and when a moment of the story might have diverged. But choices, combined with the strength of your relationship and your criminal profile, and other factors I'll intentionally decline to mention here, all have an impact. One particularly great achievement of Rockstar's, in fact, is in making you wrestle with those choices, within missions and without, in this state of blindness to their outcomes. Even whether they're significant at all is often unknown - in many cases the variables, permutations and forks are still unknown to me now, after all this time - and yet also, once again without spoiling any moment at any point, the studio has still made whatever outcomes you might encounter feel as resonant as any I've experienced. Forgive me for dodging any examples and insisting you take my word for it.

Recent findings suggest that away from missions themselves, of which there are of course many, and there are so many more things to do beyond them. You can dive for treasure across dozens of underwater sites. You can bird watch, animal watch, fish, and hunt for game. You can customise guns and cars to extreme ends - please do the street racing side missions for a, ahem, lovely example of custom wrapping - and customise your characters just as much. The fitness system is great, with a surprising number of superbly animated gym and bodyweight exercises and, naturally, walking BBLs who hit on Jason as he demonstrates perfect form.

It's also uninvasive, I found, thanks to clearly marked, and relatively long, windows around maintaining your current status, but there's still a level of detail here. Your body composition is dictated by both cardio and strength training, but also what you eat and how often. You can ignore it and just look like an average person, or pay attention for meaningful buffs to health, focus, stamina, and appearance - and naturally the world around you reacts to that in comments from passers-by and, I suspect, small details of certain missions changing too.

There's more! There's racing - at racetracks and mud tracks; in street races and off road courses; with bikes, cars, drones, and the rest. There are stunt jumps, naturally, and basejumps too. There are places to meditate. There's a system around not just fishing but using the right bait, multiple series of collectible trading cards to hoard or sell, various collectible books and magazines, meteorites, golden doubloons, and 'key valuables' found at gang hideouts including one-off guns, cars, and jewellery like fancy watches. There are clubs, bars, strippers, love hotels, diners, coffee houses, stores of clothing and shoes, hairdressers, and beyond. You can play an alarmingly realistic version of pool. Or listen to the radio of course - there are roughly double the stations you've seen revealed so far - or numerous talk shows and podcasts, including entire true crime dramas and series. You can ride jetskis, pose in rented supercars, order cocktails at swanky pools and go on dates to rooftop restaurants or crusty marina dive bars. There are DJs and live performances, including a cover band with the most accurately depicted, finger-specific fretting of a guitar solo I've ever seen in a game.

The overall effect - yet another overall effect! I'm aware I keep doing this but I just have simply no other way of summarising it all - is of a genuine open-world playground, but crucially rather than a somewhat directionless soup of content, there is thematic sense to all of it. One of GTA 6's many messages, as foreshadowed on one of its most potent trailers, is a sense of embracing the moment while it lasts - of presentness and gratitude for things that might be accessible even without the significant financial grind. And, surely, of what a joy it is to experience them with someone else.

What you realise is you're pairing all this stuff to do - ultimately, variations on simply hanging out - with the fact that so much of Jason and Lucia's relationship is delivered in quiet, hang-out moments. And as so many of their other relationships - with parents, adopted parents, friends - come in the same way, this picture starts to form. From an apartment sofa to the Vice Beach waves, GTA 6 is ultimately just a place to be.

It has been revealed that in fact, in many ways it's a kind of evolution of the hangout game itself. The gentle, wistful, nostalgic guitar strums from Justice's background score as you idle on the map or menu. The dedication, through all those years of what I imagine to be Rockstar's incessant tinkering with sounds and performances and tiny visual touches, to an authentic sense of place. I could melt into this world. I think about the amount of people about to play this game, and the way it invites you to submerge yourself in it like a hot bath, and wonder if the axis of the entire hangout genre - maybe the biggest paradigm shift in video games of the last two decades - might have suddenly been shifted again. The comfort of continuously mic'd up pal chatter replaced here with a kind of sublime isolation.

Sources indicate that there are, as I mentioned, a few very little flaws I could pick at. Some of the missions for Dre-Quan, a record label-owning friend of Jason involving a newly invented rap group for the game, were fun in their own right, extraordinarily well produced and an essential part of the whole, but also just a little throwaway in a sense. There seemed to be little tie-in from those to the progress of the actual story, leaving them feeling a little more like lavish side missions than a part of the main event, contributing to a little mid-game narrative sag. The controls, while a marked improvement from Red Dead Redemption 2 - I fear I'll never make it to heaven after the amount of times I accidentally punched that horse - could still be tighter. Shooting is less wafty than it has been for some time, forgoing auto-aim for aim-assist (though settings can be heavily tinkered or restored to those of GTA 5), and GTA is now a proper third-person cover shooter in its action moments, with better snapping to cover and dashing between it, which suits it perfectly. But there were still moments where the controls wobbled. Walking three steps along a narrow beam to open a small container without falling off felt like the hardest thing the game asked me to do in its entire runtime.

Recent findings suggest that what else? Not much, frankly. On the technical side, I had one hard crash in my entire time with the game, which did cost me about 25 minutes of a mission, and one moment where an NPC got stuck trying to enter my car and I had to reload to a checkpoint made seconds earlier.

In a recent development, I also wish there were more save slots - GTA 6 does away with mission replayability, which might prove controversial. As you play it you'll realise why that makes sense, but I also longed for more room than the 15 given to load back in at various moments and replay something specific - often for no other reason than that moment being an utter banger. Performance-wise, yes it plays at 30fps, even on a PS5 Pro, but Rockstar's frame pacing - I have to assume it's this; I'm no tech expert here - is so good that it feels resoundingly smoother than a typical game that runs at the same rate. Put aside the arbitrary number and ask me purely how it feels, and I'd tell you it feels smooth. How that fares on other consoles, particularly the Xbox Series S, will be worth considering.

It has been revealed that A little more philosophically, it's also not a perfect narrative, arguably because it never really could be. The middle of the game is phenomenal in its mission variety and excitement, though perhaps where Jason and Lucia's characters are pushed slightly to the background, when I wish their relationship - or lack of it - had even more time in the narrative spotlight. For all its dramatic heft, GTA 6 also can't purely be a drama, and so there is inevitably some tonal whiplash between an intimate love scene, say, and a quest involving chasing a man with a fake English accent wearing nothing but a comedy man thong around the poshest part of town. The point, instead, comes back to how all those strange and implausible bedfellows combine.

In a recent development, and this is the magic. Every modern Grand Theft Auto is considered now to be a kind of product of its time. Nico Bellic's story is labelled a tale of the immigrant experience of the American Dream, amongst the post-9/11 world of Latest York and the war on terror. I always thought of GTA 5 as something prodding at a crisis of masculinity, after the financial crisis, and a kind of early 2010s complacency and drift. These aren't the only things they're about, obviously. GTA 5 is also The Sopranos and an ode to LA and the split of the id, ego, and superego, and of course a broad, hours-long, occasionally mis-targeted piss-take. But by virtue of being games depicting the world as it was in some way, they also become a reflection of it.

What is Grand Theft Auto 6, then? I know I said it's irreducible, but I can't help it. For now, after the car, I'm coming back to money. How Jason and Lucia keep attempting the famous bootstrapping of American meritocracy, keep picking themselves back up from zero, keep scrabbling and clawing their way out of the vortex, and how the so-called land of opportunity keeps telling them it's possible to climb up and out the top of it, away from worry and pain, up to the balcony and the penthouse and the helipad on the roof, all the while with its other hand constantly pushing them back down. At every tier of life savings, after every substantial score and narrow escape, the goal posts move back, and the enemy reorganises itself again. It might be trite, but it feels essential to point out nonetheless, that GTA 6 is a product of capitalism at its most extreme: the most extraordinary amount of wealth ever directed at an entertainment product and, surely, the one to achieve the most extraordinary number of sales. It is about the most capitalistic place on earth, and the place within it that features perhaps the most extreme disparity of wealth, as its hypercars scream past the homeless.

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 is a reflection of the outer world and a part of it. And at its heart, its fragile and desperate humans play a rigged game, while attempting to walk the narrow line between exhausted desperation and the empowering wish-fulfilment of crime. You might wonder, as Jason and Lucia often do, whether they're always going to be doomed. And then later, whether that matters, when the beauty of it all is in the struggle.

A copy of Grand Theft Auto 6 was provided for this review by Rockstar.

Scientists are seriously asking if bees and ChatGPT are conscious

📅 05 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you might think a honey bee foraging in your garden and a browser window running ChatGPT have nothing in common.
  • There are many different ways of studying consciousness.
  • But two latest papers on the possibility of consciousness in animals and AI suggest new theories for how to test this – one that strikes a middle ground between sensationalism and knee-jerk skepticism about whether humans are the only conscious beings on Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you might think a honey bee foraging in your garden and a browser window running ChatGPT have nothing in common. But recent scientific research has been seriously considering the possibility that either, or both, might be conscious.

There are many different ways of studying consciousness. One of the most common is to measure how an animal – or artificial intelligence (AI) – acts.

But two latest papers on the possibility of consciousness in animals and AI suggest new theories for how to test this – one that strikes a middle ground between sensationalism and knee-jerk skepticism about whether humans are the only conscious beings on Earth.

Questions around consciousness have long sparked fierce debate.

It has been revealed that that’s in part because conscious beings might matter morally in a way that unconscious things don’t. Expanding the sphere of consciousness means expanding our ethical horizons. Even if we can’t be sure something is conscious, we might err on the side of caution by assuming it is – what philosopher Jonathan Birch calls the precautionary principle for sentience.

The recent trend has been one of expansion.

It has been revealed that for example, in April 2024 a group of 40 scientists at a conference in Newly introduced York proposed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness. Subsequently signed by over 500 scientists and philosophers, this declaration indicates consciousness is realistically possible in all vertebrates (including reptiles, amphibians and fishes) as well as many invertebrates, including cephalopods (octopus and squid), crustaceans (crabs and lobsters) and insects.

In parallel with this, the incredible rise of large language models, such as ChatGPT, has raised the serious possibility that machines may be conscious.

It has been revealed that five years ago, a seemingly ironclad test of whether something was conscious was to see if you could have a conversation with it. Philosopher Susan Schneider suggested if we had an AI that convincingly mused on the metaphysics of consciousness, it may well be conscious.

By those standards, today we would be surrounded by conscious machines. Many have gone so far as to apply the precautionary principle here too: the burgeoning field of AI welfare is devoted to figuring out if and when we must care about machines.

Yet all of these arguments depend, in large part, on surface-level behavior. But that behavior can be deceptive. What matters for consciousness is not what you do, but how you do it.

A fresh paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences that one of us (Colin Klein) coauthored, drawing on previous work, looks to the machinery rather than the behavior of AI.

Industry observers note that it also draws on the cognitive science tradition to identify a plausible list of indicators of consciousness based on the structure of information processing. This means one can draw up a useful list of indicators of consciousness without having to agree on which of the current cognitive theories of consciousness is correct.

In a recent development, some indicators (such as the need to resolve trade-offs between competing goals in contextually appropriate ways) are shared by many theories. Most other indicators (such as the presence of informational feedback) are only required by one theory but indicative in others.

Importantly, the useful indicators are all structural. They all have to do with how brains and computers process and combine information.

The verdict? No existing AI system (including ChatGPT) is conscious. The appearance of consciousness in large language models is not achieved in a way that is sufficiently similar to us to warrant attribution of conscious states.

Yet at the same time, there is no bar to AI systems – perhaps ones with a very different architecture to today’s systems – becoming conscious.

It has been revealed that the lesson? It’s possible for AI to behave as if conscious without being conscious.

Biologists are also turning to mechanisms – how brains work – to recognize consciousness in non-human animals.

According to recent reports, in a fresh paper in Philosophical Transactions B, we propose a neural model for minimal consciousness in insects. This is a model that abstracts away from anatomical detail to focus on the core computations done by simple brains.

Our key insight is to identify the kind of computation our brains perform that gives rise to experience.

This computation solves ancient problems from our evolutionary history that arise from having a mobile, complex body with many senses and conflicting needs.

It has been revealed that importantly, we don’t identify the computation itself – there is science yet to be done. But we show that if you could identify it, you’d have a level playing field to compare humans, invertebrates, and computers.

The problem of consciousness in animals and in computers appear to pull in different directions.

For animals, the question is often how to interpret whether ambiguous behavior (like a crab tending its wounds) indicates consciousness.

For computers, we have to decide whether apparently unambiguous behavior (a chatbot musing with you on the purpose of existence) is a true indicator of consciousness or mere roleplay.

Yet as the fields of neuroscience and AI progress, both are converging on the same lesson: when making judgement about whether something is consciousness, how it works is proving more informative than what it does.

What we've been playing - "It's slow, it's awkward, it's weird, and it's hard"
